title: 1995–2000: From Boom to Bubble
tagline: The New Economy myth · Information technology revolution · Budget surpluses · Irrational exuberance

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: These were the most brilliant six years of the postwar US economy. Real GDP grew at an average annual rate of 4.3%, and unemployment fell from 5.6% in 1995 to 4.0% in 2000 — 'full employment' was achieved on a sustained basis for the first time. Fiscal year 1998 produced the first federal surplus ($69.2 billion); 1999 and 2000 brought a record $236 billion surplus — Clinton's fiscal miracle.

'The New Economy' became the era's keyword. The combination of the IT revolution, globalization, and Fed accommodation kept inflation steady at 2–3% (CPI 2.8% in 1995, 3.4% in 2000). 'High growth, low inflation, low unemployment' broke the traditional Phillips-curve view, and Greenspan's 'productivity revolution' thesis became the consensus.

But the tail end of the boom was a bubble. When Greenspan first warned of 'irrational exuberance' in December 1996, the Nasdaq was 1,300; it peaked at 5,048 in March 2000 — a 4x gain in three years. From March 2000 the dot-com bubble burst, and the Nasdaq lost 78% over two and a half years. The 'New Economy' narrative looked absurd by 2001, but 1995–2000 was a genuine combination of real prosperity and a real bubble — the two cannot be cleanly separated.

items.body: After six Fed hikes in 1994, the economy did not crash but landed softly. 1995 GDP grew 2.7%. The Fed pivoted to cuts in July 1995 (fed funds from 6.0% to 5.25%). Greenspan delivered his 'irrational exuberance' speech on December 5, 1996, but markets shrugged it off.

items.strong: 1997–1998: Out of Deficits, Asian Crisis Spillovers
items.body: The Thai baht's collapse on July 2, 1997 triggered the Asian financial crisis, which spread to South Korea, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The Russian ruble crisis hit in July 1998. In September 1998 Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) blew up and the Fed convened 14 investment banks to organize the rescue. The Fed cut rates three times between September and November 1998 to prevent contagion. The domestic economy stayed strong: 1998 GDP +4.5%, 1999 +4.8%. Fiscal year 1998 produced the first surplus.

1999 GDP grew 4.8% and CPI was 2.2%; Y2K fears drove an explosion in IT capex. The Financial Services Modernization Act (November 12, 1999) repealed Glass-Steagall. The Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 on March 10, 2000. The Fed hiked six times from June 1999 to May 2000 (5.0% to 6.5%), puncturing the bubble. 2000 GDP grew 4.1%, but the Nasdaq fell over 50% within the year.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: Information Revolution and Services
body: The information technology revolution was the structural through-line. Windows 95 launched, Netscape went public, and Amazon was founded in 1995; Google was founded in 1998; at the 2000 peak, tech stocks were ~35% of S&P 500 market cap. Private IT investment grew at an annualized 14% rate, rising from 3.5% of GDP in 1995 to 5% in 2000.

Finance and real estate kept expanding — from 18% of GDP in 1994 to 20% in 2000. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of November 1999 repealed Glass-Steagall, permitting commercial banks, investment banks, and insurers to operate under a single roof — the institutional setup for the 2008 crisis.

Globalization accelerated: the WTO was established on January 1, 1995; China's WTO accession talks concluded in December 1999; the US granted China Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) in October 2000. Chinese exports rose from $148.7 billion in 1995 to $249.2 billion in 2000, and the US trade deficit with China rose from $33.9 billion to $83.8 billion.

Within the GDP breakdown, corporate profits' share declined: listed-company profits as a share of GDP gradually fell from their 1994 peak. From 1996 to 2000, cumulative pre-tax corporate profit growth trailed GDP growth — the 'New Economy' boom was more about tech-stock valuations than overall earnings.

sections.heading: Financial Regulation: The End of Deregulation
body: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA), signed November 12, 1999, repealed the Glass-Steagall ban on combining banking, securities, and insurance, permitting financial holding companies. Citigroup had already built a de facto universal-bank model through its 1998 merger with Travelers Group; GLBA was the legal confirmation.

The Commodity Futures Modernization Act (CFMA), signed December 21, 2000, exempted OTC derivatives — including credit default swaps — from SEC and CFTC oversight. This regulatory vacuum would be fully exploited in the 2007–2008 crisis.
These two laws marked the high-water mark of the 'Clinton–Greenspan–Rubin' neoliberal approach to financial regulation.
